reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes BitClub Network through a large team structure, sponsored business lines, rank-based leadership and extraordinary Bitcoin income claims. The interview presents claims of 8–10 bitcoins per day and 300 bitcoins per month positively, while the video repeatedly displays a registration call to action directing viewers to a link below the video.

citations.quote: I have sponsored is business line. We are 25 business rows. Is there 25 business lines? Total 20.000 people. So, the team is 20.000 people.
Now there are 20 000 people in our team. And our team has 6 monster builders.
Every day you get 8 to 10 bitcoins in your income. One month, 300 bitcoins. The highest salary is 300 bitcoins per month.

opening.argument: Judge the income discussion by what it actually says. The interviewer asks for the largest investment the guest remembers within his team, not a return a viewer should expect. The answer calls 300 bitcoins per month the highest salary, which describes an extreme case rather than a guaranteed result. The title asks how much someone can earn, but neither that question nor the reported maximum establishes that viewers will earn it. The description's invitation to learn about cryptocurrency is promotional; it still does not turn this interview answer into a promise of returns.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opposing account quotes a striking income figure, but its own quotation calls it the highest salary, not a typical or promised payment. It also treats the team's size as proof of how earnings work; a headcount does not establish a commission rule. The registration prompt deserves scrutiny, but it does not itself specify a deposit or guarantee a return.

citations.quote: Every day you get 8 to 10 bitcoins in your income. One month, 300 bitcoins. The highest salary is 300 bitcoins per month.
Now there are 20 000 people in our team. And our team has 6 monster builders.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Calling the figure a maximum does not erase the direct, unqualified statement, “Every day you get 8 to 10 bitcoins in your income.” Nor is this detached market analysis: the speaker describes sponsored business lines and a 20,000-person team, while the video displays a registration prompt. The defense identifies no actual risk warning or disclaimer in those passages.

opening.argument: This is presented as an event interview, with the host asking a guest to introduce himself and describe his experience. The questions move from whether people in Japan know Bitcoin to what the guest remembers about investments in his team; the closing asks viewers for comments and likes. That format gives a viewer information about one participant's account, not instructions to enter a transaction. The registration text visible in the frame is promotional context, but the spoken exchange does not walk viewers through paying, supplying credentials or obtaining the reported income.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opposing account compresses interview answers about team size, rank and a reported income maximum into a claim that viewers are being offered those earnings. Yet the host explicitly asks about what happened within the guest's structure, and the exchange ends by requesting comments and likes. The on-screen registration prompt is real, but it does not make every answer in the interview a promise to the viewer.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: An interview format does not make this an operational lesson. The title explicitly promises a discussion of earning Bitcoin with BitClub Network; the guest discusses sponsored business lines and team size, and the income claim is stated in the second person. A registration prompt remains on-screen during the interview. Those details make the favorable account of the opportunity part of a solicitation, not merely a neutral demonstration.

opening.argument: The visible business context is a cryptocurrency opportunity being discussed at an event. The guest mentions a sponsored business line and a large team, but those phrases alone do not specify a payment for recruiting anyone, a tiered commission formula or a required viewer deposit. Even the question about the largest investment concerns someone in the guest's structure, not a sum the audience is told to send. The description points to a site, and the frame asks viewers to register; neither supplied item shows what registration requires. That leaves the alleged financial mechanism unestablished by this video.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opposing account identifies business rows, a team and leadership ranks, but does not quote a rule tying anyone's income to recruiting another person. It also cites a registration prompt without showing the terms behind that link. The income number is concerning, yet an extraordinary claim is not, by itself, evidence of the particular commission mechanism alleged here.

The description directs viewers to a start link, while the frame calls for registration. The absence of displayed payment terms does not make that combination ordinary commerce.
